```{r data-import-setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
options(digits = 3)
```

`recipe()` accepts a `phyloseq` or `TreeSummarizedExperiment` object. These
containers connect an abundance matrix to sample metadata and, when available,
taxonomy. Import files with the tools supplied by `phyloseq` or `mia`, then
inspect the resulting object before configuring an analysis.

Importing data does not establish that their units, experimental design or
taxonomic annotations are appropriate for a particular differential-abundance
method.

## Start with an existing phyloseq object

The package includes `metaHIV_phy`, with its recorded sample metadata and
taxonomy. No statistical model is needed to inspect the data or define
preprocessing steps.

```{r data-import-recipe}
library(dar)
data("metaHIV_phy", package = "dar")

rec <- recipe(metaHIV_phy)
rec
```

`recipe()` also accepts a `phyloseq` object whose stored abundance matrix has
samples in rows: the accessors below return one consistent orientation. When
constructing your own `phyloseq` object, set `taxa_are_rows` to match the actual
matrix, rather than changing this flag without transposing the data.

## Inspect samples, taxonomy and abundances

Use the dar accessors explicitly when other attached packages export functions
with the same names.

```{r data-import-accessors}
samples <- dar::sample_data(rec)
taxonomy <- dar::tax_table(rec)
abundances <- dar::otu_table(rec)

head(samples[c("sample_id", "RiskGroup2")])
head(taxonomy)
abundances[seq_len(6), seq_len(5)]
```

The accessors expose the complete stored components, independently of the
target or taxonomic rank later selected with `add_model()`:

- `sample_data()` returns `sample_id` followed by all sample metadata columns,
  in `phyloseq::sample_names()` order.
- `tax_table()` returns `taxa_id` followed by all taxonomic ranks, in
  `phyloseq::taxa_names()` order.
- `otu_table()` returns one row per taxon, with `taxa_id` first and one column
  per sample. Taxon and sample order match the other two accessors.

```{r data-import-alignment}
stopifnot(
  identical(colnames(abundances)[-1], samples$sample_id),
  identical(abundances$taxa_id, taxonomy$taxa_id)
)
```

Keep sample and taxon identifiers unique and consistent across input files.
Taxonomic labels are annotations, not replacements for feature identifiers:
several features can share a species name. Inspect missing annotations and use
standard rank names such as `Kingdom`, `Genus` and `Species`.

If metadata or taxonomy is absent, the corresponding accessor returns an
ID-only tibble. That is sufficient for inspection, but it does not supply the
real covariates or taxonomic rank needed by a model. Add genuine study metadata
before calling `add_model()`; do not manufacture groups just to make an example
run.

## Extract the shared taxonomic analysis view

Selecting `tax_level = "Genus"` with `add_model()` does not replace the stored
features returned by `otu_table()`. `tidy_abundance()` instead exposes the
shared analysis view: counts are summed through the selected rank, using the
same taxon identities as differential-abundance results. Features with the
same label but different lineages remain distinct analysis units.

```{r data-import-analysis-view}
genus_rec <- recipe(metaHIV_phy) |>
  add_model(~ RiskGroup2, targets = "RiskGroup2", tax_level = "Genus")

genus_abundances <- tidy_abundance(genus_rec, metadata = "RiskGroup2")
head(genus_abundances)
data.frame(
  stored_features = nrow(dar::otu_table(genus_rec)),
  analysis_taxa = dplyr::n_distinct(genus_abundances$taxa_id)
)
```

The long table has one row per taxon and sample, with `taxa_id`, `taxa`,
`sample_id` and `abundance`. Taxonomy has a `taxonomy_` prefix and selected
sample metadata a `metadata_` prefix, so annotations cannot overwrite these
columns. Supply original metadata names to `metadata`; `NULL` includes all
metadata and `character(0)` excludes them. Lineage is retained through the
selected rank; lower ranks removed by aggregation remain missing.

For within-sample fractions, select `transform = "compositional"`. The
denominator includes **all shared analysis taxa**, before selecting taxon IDs;
fractions of a displayed subset need not sum to one.

```{r data-import-analysis-fractions}
selected_ids <- head(unique(genus_abundances$taxa_id), 2)
fractions <- tidy_abundance(
  genus_rec, taxa_ids = selected_ids,
  transform = "compositional", metadata = "RiskGroup2"
)
head(fractions)
```

The default `transform = "identity"` preserves the stored abundance scale
while summing aggregated features. Extraction from an unprepared recipe does
not execute pending steps. A prepared recipe includes common preprocessing
and the shared model cohort, but this view does not reproduce method-specific
filtering, rarefaction or transformations. It is not a table of adjusted
predictions. For paired graphics, include the actual visit and participant
columns in `metadata` and use them to group descriptive trajectories.

## Import a BIOM table

This example uses a file distributed with `phyloseq`, without downloading data.
The importer reads the sample metadata already present in that file.

```{r data-import-biom}
biom_file <- system.file(
  "extdata", "rich_dense_otu_table.biom", package = "phyloseq"
)

phy <- phyloseq::import_biom(
  biom_file,
  parseFunction = phyloseq::parse_taxonomy_greengenes
)
biom_rec <- recipe(phy)
head(dar::sample_data(biom_rec))
head(dar::tax_table(biom_rec))
```

The same file can be imported as a `TreeSummarizedExperiment`. Rows of a TSE
represent features, columns represent samples, `rowData()` holds feature
annotations and `colData()` holds sample metadata.

```{r data-import-tse}
tse <- mia::importBIOM(biom_file)

# This bundled example contains these seven ranks, in this order.
colnames(SummarizedExperiment::rowData(tse)) <- c(
  "Kingdom", "Phylum", "Class", "Order", "Family", "Genus", "Species"
)

tse_rec <- recipe(tse)
head(dar::tax_table(tse_rec))
```

The rank relabeling above is specific to this file. Inspect the annotations in
your own data instead of assigning rank names by position without checking
their meaning. A TSE input is converted internally to `phyloseq`; if the
intended abundance table is not the default assay, select it explicitly with
`mia::convertToPhyloseq(..., assay.type = "your_assay")` before creating the
recipe.

For other formats, consult the importers' documentation rather than treating
all formats as equivalent:

- `phyloseq::import_qiime()` reads legacy QIIME tables;
  `mia::importQIIME2()` reads QIIME 2 artifacts.
- `phyloseq::import_mothur()` and `mia::importMothur()` read the supported
  mothur files.
- `mia::importMetaPhlAn()` reads MetaPhlAn abundance profiles.

For example, open the installed help with
`help("importQIIME2", package = "mia")` or
`help("import_biom", package = "phyloseq")`.

## Check the measurement scale

An abundance matrix can contain raw read counts, proportions, percentages or
other transformed values. These are not interchangeable inputs. In particular,
MetaPhlAn relative-abundance profiles are not raw read counts. Neither importing
them nor converting their container makes them suitable for a count-based
model; rounding percentages does not recover read counts.

Check the provenance and assay units, not just whether values happen to be
integers. Retain raw counts when they are available and choose a method whose
input requirements match the measurements. Missing values are also distinct
from observed zeros.

For QC and filtering, continue with
[Quality control and preprocessing](filtering_subsetting.html).
For formulas, target variables and engine compatibility, see
[Statistical models and contrasts](statistical_models.html).
